title: Stage-adaptive audio diffusion modeling
summary: Recent progress in diffusion-based audio generation and restoration has substantially improved performance across heterogeneous conditioning regimes, including text-conditioned audio generation and audio-conditioned super-resolution. However, training audio diffusion models remains computationally expensive, and most existing pipelines still rely on static optimization recipes that treat the relative importance of training signals as fixed throughout learning. In this work, we argue that a major source of inefficiency lies in the evolving balance between semantic acquisition and generation-oriented refinement. Early training places stronger emphasis on acquiring condition-aligned semantic structure and coarse global organization, whereas later training increasingly emphasizes temporal consistency, perceptual fidelity, and fine-detail refinement. To characterize this evolving balance, we introduce a progress-based regime variable derived from the training-time slope of an SSL-space discrepancy, which measures semantic progress during training. Based on this signal, we develop three complementary stage-aware mechanisms: decayed SSL guidance for early semantic bootstrapping, self-adaptive timestep sampling driven by the regime variable, and structure-aware regularization activated from convergent grouped organization in parameter space. We evaluate these mechanisms on text-conditioned audio generation and audio-conditioned super-resolution. Across both settings, the proposed stage-aware strategies improve convergence behavior and yield gains on the primary generation and spectral reconstruction metrics over standard static baselines. These results support the view that efficient audio diffusion training can benefit from treating external guidance, internal organization, and optimization emphasis as stage-dependent components rather than fixed ingredients.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces stage-aware training mechanisms for audio diffusion models that adaptively adjust optimization emphasis (semantic acquisition vs. fine-detail refinement) based on a progress-based regime variable derived from SSL-space discrepancy, improving convergence and performance on text-conditioned audio generation and audio-conditioned super-resolution tasks.
AI.motivation: Training audio diffusion models is computationally expensive and existing pipelines use static optimization recipes that treat the relative importance of training signals as fixed throughout learning, ignoring the evolving balance between semantic acquisition (early) and generation-oriented refinement (later).
AI.method: Introduces a progress-based regime variable derived from the training-time slope of an SSL-space discrepancy to characterize semantic progress. Develops three stage-aware mechanisms: (1) decayed SSL guidance for early semantic bootstrapping, (2) self-adaptive timestep sampling driven by the regime variable, and (3) structure-aware regularization activated from convergent grouped organization in parameter space.
AI.result: Across text-conditioned audio generation and audio-conditioned super-resolution, the stage-aware strategies improve convergence behavior and yield gains on primary generation and spectral reconstruction metrics over standard static baselines.
AI.conclusion: Efficient audio diffusion training benefits from treating external guidance, internal organization, and optimization emphasis as stage-dependent components rather than fixed ingredients.

title: VocalParse: Towards Unified and Scalable Singing Voice Transcription with Large Audio Language Models
summary: High-quality singing annotations are fundamental to modern Singing Voice Synthesis (SVS) systems. However, obtaining these annotations at scale through manual labeling is unrealistic due to the substantial labor and musical expertise required, making automatic annotation highly necessary. Despite their utility, current automatic transcription systems face significant challenges: they often rely on complex multi-stage pipelines, struggle to recover text-note alignments, and exhibit poor generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) singing data. To alleviate these issues, we present VocalParse, a unified singing voice transcription (SVT) model built upon a Large Audio Language Model (LALM). Specifically, our novel contribution is to introduce an interleaved prompting formulation that jointly models lyrics, melody, and word-note correspondence, yielding a generated sequence that directly maps to a structured musical score. Furthermore, we propose a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) style prompting strategy, which decodes lyrics first as a semantic scaffold, significantly mitigating the context disruption problem while preserving the structural benefits of interleaved generation. Experiments demonstrate that VocalParse achieves state-of-the-art SVT performance on multiple singing datasets. The source code and checkpoint are available at https://github.com/pymaster17/VocalParse.

AI.tldr: VocalParse is a unified singing voice transcription model using a Large Audio Language Model with interleaved prompting for lyrics, melody, and word-note alignment, plus a Chain-of-Thought strategy to improve transcription accuracy. It achieves SOTA results on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Manual annotation of singing data for SVS is labor-intensive and requires musical expertise; existing automatic transcription systems rely on complex multi-stage pipelines, struggle with text-note alignment recovery, and generalize poorly to out-of-distribution singing data.
AI.method: VocalParse is built upon a Large Audio Language Model (LALM). It introduces (1) an interleaved prompting formulation that jointly models lyrics, melody, and word-note correspondence to directly map to a structured musical score, and (2) a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) style prompting strategy that decodes lyrics first as a semantic scaffold to reduce context disruption while preserving interleaved generation benefits.
AI.result: VocalParse achieves state-of-the-art Singing Voice Transcription performance on multiple singing datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified model with interleaved prompting and CoT strategy effectively addresses key limitations of prior SVT systems, delivering superior transcription quality.

title: Safety by Invariance, Liveness through Refinement: Heterogeneous Contract Framework for Co-Design of Layered Control
summary: Real-world control systems must achieve long-horizon objectives (liveness) while respecting continuous-time safety constraints, a combination that motivates hierarchical layered control architectures (LCAs). Existing LCA research, however, lacks (i) a uniform specification language across discrete planning and continuous execution, (ii) formal guarantees that specifications are preserved when interconnecting subsystems at heterogeneous time scales, and (iii) compositional separation between layers, owing to reliance on naive input-filtering laws. This paper addresses all three gaps by importing the safety--liveness decomposition into a heterogeneous assume--guarantee framework: \emph{safety is enforced by invariance} at the continuous-time layer, while \emph{liveness is achieved through refinement} at the discrete-time layer, with inter-layer coordination formalized via vertical refinement and timing-compatibility conditions. We instantiate this contract with a novel LCA combining an MPC planner, an input-to-state stabilizing (ISS) low-level controller, and a reference-governor bridge, and validate it on a Hybrid Energy Storage System (HESS) comprising a battery and a supercapacitor.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hierarchical layered control architecture (LCA) that formally separates safety (continuous-time invariance) from liveness (discrete-time refinement) using an assume-guarantee framework, demonstrated on a Hybrid Energy Storage System.
AI.motivation: Existing LCA research lacks a uniform specification language across discrete planning and continuous execution, formal guarantees across heterogeneous time scales, and compositional separation between layers due to naive input-filtering.
AI.method: The authors decompose safety and liveness into a heterogeneous assume-guarantee framework: safety is enforced by invariance at the continuous-time layer, liveness by refinement at the discrete-time layer, with inter-layer coordination via vertical refinement and timing-compatibility conditions. The framework is instantiated with an MPC planner, an ISS low-level controller, and a reference-governor bridge.
AI.result: The approach is validated on a Hybrid Energy Storage System (HESS) with a battery and supercapacitor.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides formal compositional guarantees for safety and liveness in hierarchical control by bridging continuous-time and discrete-time layers through vertical refinement and timing compatibility.

title: Hearing the Ocean: Bio-inspired Gammatone-CNN framework for Robust Underwater Acoustic Target Classification
summary: This study presents a bio inspired signal processing framework for robust Underwater Acoustic Target Recognition (UATR). The latest state of the art methods often fail to resolve dense low frequency harmonic structures in vessel propulsion signals under high noise conditions, which is addressed by the proposed framework using a biologically inspired Gammatone filter bank that emulates the cochlea nonlinear frequency selectivity. By distributing filters according to the Equivalent Rectangular Bandwidth (ERB) scale, the framework achieves a high fidelity representation of engine radiated tonals while effectively suppressing isotropic ambient interference. The resulting Cochleagram features are processed by a lightweight, custom designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that leverages large receptive fields to integrate spectral-temporal continuities. Experimental results on the VTUAD dataset demonstrate a state of the art classification accuracy of 98.41%, outperforming Continuous Wavelet Transform and Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients baselines by 3.5% and 7.7% respectively. Furthermore, the framework achieves an inference latency of only 0.77 ms and a 0.971 Cohen Kappa score, validating its efficacy for real time deployment on autonomous, low-power sonar hardware.

AI.tldr: A bio-inspired UATR framework using Gammatone filter bank (ERB-scaled) and lightweight CNN achieves 98.41% accuracy, 0.77 ms latency, and 0.971 Cohen Kappa on VTUAD dataset, outperforming CWT and MFCC baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing UATR methods fail to resolve dense low-frequency harmonic structures in vessel propulsion signals under high noise conditions.
AI.method: Gammatone filter bank based on ERB scale for cochlea-mimicking frequency selectivity → Cochleagram features → lightweight CNN with large receptive fields for spectral-temporal integration.
AI.result: 98.41% accuracy (3.5% over CWT, 7.7% over MFCC), 0.77 ms inference latency, 0.971 Cohen Kappa on VTUAD dataset.
AI.conclusion: The framework is effective for real-time deployment on autonomous, low-power sonar hardware.

title: Thinking fast and slow -- decision intelligence for power systems
comment: 5 pages, This work has been submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Decision-making in power systems spans multiple timescales - from milliseconds to prevent surges, to seconds to balance frequency and protect grid assets, to minutes for real-time energy balancing, to day-ahead, seasonal, and long-term planning. Growing uncertainty and complexity, driven by intermittent renewables and distributed energy resources (DER), demand fresh approaches to power system intelligence and architecture. Daniel Kahneman describes the interplay of two systems of human decision-making: System 1 that is fast, intuitive, experience based, reactive, and System 2 that is slow, deliberate, analytical. Similarly, octopus intelligence illustrates a model for distributed yet coordinated decision-making between central and edge intelligence. Future power systems must embed coordinated intelligence that operates across diverse timescales and with placement at both edge and centralized levels. This paper maps decision-intelligence in power systems against System 1 and 2 and edge-central architecture paradigms based on the trade-offs inherent in decision making such as speed/latency, energy cost/compute, accuracy, and robustness. The framework inspires an agentic intelligence architecture - laying the foundation for trustworthy, autonomous power systems of the future.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework mapping power system decision-intelligence to Kahneman's System 1 (fast, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, analytical) thinking, combined with edge-central architecture paradigms inspired by octopus intelligence, to enable trustworthy autonomous power systems across multiple timescales.
AI.motivation: Growing uncertainty and complexity from intermittent renewables and distributed energy resources (DER) demand fresh approaches to power system intelligence and architecture, as traditional decision-making across multiple timescales (milliseconds to long-term planning) faces challenges in speed, accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency.
AI.method: The paper maps decision-intelligence in power systems against Kahneman's System 1 (fast, intuitive, reactive) and System 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical) paradigms, combined with an octopus-inspired edge-central distributed coordination architecture, analyzing trade-offs in speed/latency, energy cost/compute, accuracy, and robustness.
AI.result: A framework that inspires an agentic intelligence architecture, laying the foundation for trustworthy, autonomous power systems of the future by balancing trade-offs inherent in decision-making across timescales and placement levels.
AI.conclusion: Embedding coordinated intelligence at both edge and centralized levels, operating across diverse timescales, is essential for future power systems; the proposed framework provides a foundation for trustworthy autonomous systems.

title: Empirical Study of Pop and Jazz Mix Ratios for Genre-Adaptive Chord Generation
comment: 3 figures, 5 tables. Companion HuggingFace models: https://huggingface.co/PearlLeeStudio
summary: Chord progression generation is practically important but understudied. Most large-scale symbolic music systems target melody, multi-track arrangement, or audio synthesis, and chord-only models tend to be relegated to conditioning components inside larger pipelines. This paper treats chord generation as a standalone task and addresses a question that arises whenever such a model is adapted across genres: how much old-domain data must be retained during fine-tuning to acquire a new domain without forgetting the old? I study jazz fine-tuning starting from a pop-pretrained 25M-parameter Music Transformer (84.24% top-1 chord accuracy on a held-out pop test set). The available jazz corpus is an order of magnitude smaller than the pop corpus, so every fine-tune run uses all 1,513 jazz training sequences. The swept variable is the volume of pop "rehearsal" data mixed alongside, taking values in {0, 1K, 2.5K, 5K, 10K}. Every fine-tuned model gains 7 to 9 points of jazz top-1. Pop accuracy collapses by 2.14 points under jazz-only fine-tuning, recovers to baseline at approximately 2.5K rehearsal samples (1.65x the jazz volume), and saturates beyond that point. A complementary observation: the metric-best run (F3, 2.5K mix) is not always the perceptually preferred one. The pop-leaning (10K) and jazz-leaning (1K) endpoints carry more committed stylistic identities that the author more often selects as finished output in informal listening. I discuss what this suggests for music co-creation tools but make no perceptual claim, since no formal listening study has been conducted. All six checkpoints are released on the HuggingFace Hub at https://huggingface.co/PearlLeeStudio.

AI.tldr: This paper studies chord progression generation as a standalone task, examining how much old-domain (pop) data must be retained when fine-tuning a Music Transformer on a new domain (jazz) to avoid catastrophic forgetting. Using a 25M-parameter model pretrained on pop music, the author fine-tunes on a small jazz corpus while mixing in varying amounts of pop rehearsal data. Results show that ~2.5K pop samples (1.65× the jazz volume) restores pop accuracy to baseline, but the perceptually preferred outputs often lean toward stylistic extremes rather than the metric-best balanced mix.
AI.motivation: Chord progression generation is understudied compared to melody or multi-track systems; chord models are often relegated to conditioning components. The author wants to treat chord generation as a standalone task and investigate how to adapt such models across genres without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: A 25M-parameter Music Transformer is pretrained on pop music (84.24% top-1 chord accuracy on held-out pop test set). Fine-tuning is performed on a small jazz corpus (1,513 training sequences) while mixing varying amounts of pop "rehearsal" data (0, 1K, 2.5K, 5K, 10K samples). The variable swept is the volume of pop rehearsal data mixed alongside the jazz data during fine-tuning.
AI.result: All fine-tuned models gain 7-9 points of jazz top-1 accuracy. Pop accuracy collapses by 2.14 points under jazz-only fine-tuning, recovers to baseline at ~2.5K rehearsal samples (1.65× the jazz volume), and saturates beyond that. The metric-best run (2.5K mix) is not always perceptually preferred; stylistic extremes (pop-leaning 10K, jazz-leaning 1K) are more often selected as finished output in informal listening.
AI.conclusion: There is a trade-off between optimal metrics and perceived stylistic identity in genre-adaptive chord generation. The author discusses implications for music co-creation tools but makes no formal perceptual claim as no listening study was conducted. All six checkpoints are publicly released.

title: Building Power Grid Models from Open Data: A Complete Pipeline from OpenStreetMap to Optimal Power Flow
comment: All models are publicly released at https://github.com/microsoft/GridSFM
summary: Access to realistic transmission grid models is essential for power systems research, yet detailed network data in the United States remains restricted under critical-infrastructure regulations. We present a pipeline that constructs complete, OPF-solvable transmission network models entirely from publicly available data. The five-stage pipeline (1) extracts power infrastructure from OpenStreetMap via a local Overpass API instance, (2) reconstructs bus-branch topology through voltage inference, line merging, and transformer detection, (3) estimates electrical parameters using voltage-class lookup tables calibrated with U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) plant-level data, (4) allocates hourly demand from EIA-930 to individual buses using US Census population as a spatial proxy, and (5) solves both DC and AC optimal power flow using PowerModels.jl with a progressive relaxation strategy that automatically loosens constraints on imprecise models. We validate the pipeline on all 48 contiguous US states and six multi-state regions, including the full Western (5,076 buses) and Eastern (21,697 buses) Interconnections. Of the 48 single-state models, 42 (88%) converge at the strictest relaxation level for AC-OPF at peak hour and 44 (92%) off-peak. Dispatch costs (median $22/MWh) and system losses (median 1.0%) are consistent with real wholesale-market outcomes. The pipeline relies exclusively on open data sources, enabling reproducible grid analysis without proprietary data. All 54 models (48 single-state and 6 multi-state) are publicly released at https://github.com/microsoft/GridSFM.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an open-source pipeline that constructs complete, OPF-solvable transmission network models (bus-branch topology, electrical parameters, demand allocation) entirely from publicly available data (OpenStreetMap, EIA, US Census), validated on 48 US states and 6 multi-state regions, achieving high AC-OPF convergence rates with dispatch costs and losses consistent with real market outcomes.
AI.motivation: Realistic transmission grid models are essential for power systems research, but detailed network data in the US is restricted under critical-infrastructure regulations, creating a need for reproducible models built from open data.
AI.method: A five-stage pipeline: (1) extract power infrastructure from OpenStreetMap via local Overpass API, (2) reconstruct bus-branch topology via voltage inference, line merging, and transformer detection, (3) estimate electrical parameters using voltage-class lookup tables calibrated with EIA plant data, (4) allocate hourly EIA-930 demand to buses using US Census population as spatial proxy, (5) solve DC/AC OPF using PowerModels.jl with progressive relaxation to handle imprecise models.
AI.result: Validated on 48 US states and 6 multi-state regions (Western 5,076 buses, Eastern 21,697 buses). 42/48 single-state models converge at strictest relaxation for AC-OPF peak hour (88%), 44/48 off-peak (92%). Median dispatch cost $22/MWh, median losses 1.0%, consistent with real wholesale-market data.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline enables fully reproducible, open-data-based transmission grid modeling without proprietary data. All 54 models are publicly released at https://github.com/microsoft/GridSFM.

title: Adaptive Diagonal Loading for Norm Constrained Beamforming
summary: Reliable adaptive beamforming is critical for large microphone arrays operating in highly dynamic acoustic environments. In scenarios characterized by fast-moving talkers and interferers, the available sample support for estimating the spatial correlation matrix is often snapshot-deficient. This deficiency, coupled with array imperfections, degrades the White Noise Gain (WNG), leading to severe target signal cancellation. To ensure stable and robust beamforming, we propose a novel adaptive diagonal loading method that guarantees the WNG remains strictly within specified bounds. By leveraging the Kantorovich inequality, we map the desired WNG to a strict upper bound on the condition number of the correlation matrix. Furthermore, we present three estimation techniques for the adaptive loading level, ranging from trace-based bounding to exact eigenvalue decomposition, offering scalable computational complexities of $\mathcal{O}(M)$, $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$, and $\mathcal{O}(M^3)$. Our approach demonstrates highly stable beamforming under fast-changing interference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive diagonal loading method for large microphone arrays that guarantees White Noise Gain (WNG) remains within strict bounds under snapshot-deficient conditions, using the Kantorovich inequality to map WNG to a condition number bound, with three estimation techniques offering O(M), O(M²), and O(M³) complexities.
AI.motivation: Reliable adaptive beamforming is critical for large microphone arrays in highly dynamic acoustic environments with fast-moving talkers and interferers, where snapshot-deficient sample support and array imperfections degrade the White Noise Gain (WNG) and cause target signal cancellation.
AI.method: A novel adaptive diagonal loading method that guarantees WNG within specified bounds by using the Kantorovich inequality to map desired WNG to a strict upper bound on the condition number of the correlation matrix, with three estimation techniques (trace-based bounding, intermediate, and exact eigenvalue decomposition) offering scalable O(M), O(M²), and O(M³) computational complexities.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates highly stable beamforming under fast-changing interference conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive diagonal loading method effectively ensures robust beamforming by strictly bounding WNG via condition number control, with scalable complexity options suitable for real-time applications.

title: StormWave: An Open-Source Portable SDR Platform for Over-the-Air Resilience Evaluation of Terrestrial and Aerial Communications
summary: This paper presents \emph{StormWave}, an open-source, portable software-defined Radio Frequency (RF) interference generation and monitoring platform designed for realistic field-based evaluation of the resilience of wireless communication systems. StormWave enables seamless composition and runtime switching among a wide range of narrowband and wideband waveforms, while supporting multiple digital modulations, adaptive coding, and multi-radio orchestration with real-time spectrum visualization. We evaluate the effectiveness of StormWave through both outdoor ground and air-to-air (A2A) experiments. Ground experiments demonstrate clear waveform- and modulation-dependent interference effects under realistic propagation conditions, while A2A experiments reveal pronounced distance-dependent constellation distortion and access-symbol degradation under active interference. The StormWave source code will be released to the community, with the expectation that StormWave will be used as a flexible, extensible, and field-ready platform for systematically validating interference resilience of wireless systems under realistic operating conditions.

AI.tldr: StormWave is an open-source, portable software-defined RF platform for generating and monitoring interference, enabling realistic field-based evaluation of wireless communication system resilience. It supports waveform composition, runtime switching, multiple digital modulations, adaptive coding, and multi-radio orchestration with real-time spectrum visualization. Ground and air-to-air experiments validate its effectiveness in demonstrating waveform/modulation-dependent interference effects and distance-dependent constellation distortion.
AI.motivation: To enable realistic field-based evaluation of wireless communication system resilience against RF interference, addressing the need for a flexible, portable, and open-source platform that can generate and monitor diverse interference waveforms under real-world propagation conditions.
AI.method: StormWave is a software-defined platform supporting seamless composition and runtime switching among narrowband/wideband waveforms, multiple digital modulations, adaptive coding, multi-radio orchestration, and real-time spectrum visualization. Validation includes outdoor ground experiments (waveform-/modulation-dependent effects) and air-to-air experiments (distance-dependent constellation distortion and access-symbol degradation).
AI.result: Ground experiments: clear waveform- and modulation-dependent interference effects under realistic propagation. A2A experiments: pronounced distance-dependent constellation distortion and access-symbol degradation under active interference.
AI.conclusion: StormWave is a flexible, extensible, field-ready platform for systematically validating interference resilience of wireless systems under realistic operating conditions. Source code will be released to the community.

title: JASTIN: Aligning LLMs for Zero-Shot Audio and Speech Evaluation via Natural Language Instructions
summary: The rapid advancement of generative audio models has outpaced the development of robust evaluation methodologies. Existing objective metrics and general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often struggle with domain generalization, zero-shot capabilities, and instructional flexibility. To address these bottlenecks, we propose JASTIN, a generalizable, instruction-driven audio evaluation framework that formulates audio assessment as a self-instructed reasoning task. JASTIN bridges a frozen high-performance audio encoder with a fine-tuned LLM backbone via a trainable audio adapter. To ensure robust zero-shot generalization, we introduce a comprehensive instruction following data preparation pipeline, incorporating Multi-Source, Multi-Task, Multi-Calibration, and Multi-Description data. Experimental results demonstrate that JASTIN achieves state-of-the-art Pearson and Spearman correlations with human subjective ratings. It consistently outperforms general MLLMs across speech, sound, music, and out-of-domain evaluation tasks without the need for task-specific retraining.

AI.tldr: JASTIN is a generalizable, instruction-driven audio evaluation framework that uses a frozen audio encoder + trainable adapter + fine-tuned LLM to assess speech, sound, and music, achieving SOTA correlation with human ratings across domains without task-specific retraining.
AI.motivation: Generative audio models have advanced rapidly, but evaluation methodologies lag behind. Existing objective metrics and MLLMs suffer from poor domain generalization, zero-shot capabilities, and limited instructional flexibility.
AI.method: JASTIN bridges a frozen high-performance audio encoder with a fine-tuned LLM backbone via a trainable audio adapter. It uses a self-instructed reasoning formulation with a multi-source, multi-task, multi-calibration, multi-description data preparation pipeline for robust zero-shot generalization.
AI.result: JASTIN achieves state-of-the-art Pearson and Spearman correlations with human subjective ratings, consistently outperforming general MLLMs across speech, sound, music, and out-of-domain evaluation tasks without task-specific retraining.
AI.conclusion: JASTIN provides a robust and flexible solution for audio evaluation that generalizes across domains and tasks, eliminating the need for task-specific retraining while aligning closely with human perception.

title: Dynamic Quantum-Assisted Co-Design of Control Tuning and Lyapunov Stability Synthesis for Nonlinear Systems
summary: This paper proposes a dynamic quantum-assisted co-design framework for nonlinear closed-loop systems in which controller parameters and Lyapunov-certificate parameters are redesigned jointly at successive decision epochs. Unlike conventional nonlinear control designs that typically tune controller gains offline and verify stability separately, the proposed method embeds performance improvement and Lyapunov-based stability synthesis within a unified online optimization loop. The main novelty is a two-step computational structure that first contracts the continuous admissible search region around the current operating condition using a Black-Hole-based calibration procedure and then constructs a finite binary representation only over this calibrated region. The encoded objective is obtained from sampled nonlinear closed-loop evaluations and approximated by a local quadratic pseudo-Boolean surrogate, enabling an Ising-type Hamiltonian representation suitable for quantum-assisted optimization. Quantum imaginary time evolution is then used to explore the encoded Hamiltonian, and the resulting candidate bitstrings are decoded into continuous controller and Lyapunov parameters. To reduce dependence on the surrogate model, the decoded candidates are re-evaluated using the original nonlinear closed-loop cost and Lyapunov penalties before the final update is applied. The framework can accommodate different Lyapunov decay specifications by modifying the stability penalty and is validated on first-order nonlinear consensus, second-order nonlinear consensus, and induction-motor drive control examples. The implementation code used to generate the reported results is available at \href{https://github.com/LSU-RAISE-LAB/DQCLS-NS}{GitHub}.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dynamic quantum-assisted co-design framework for nonlinear closed-loop systems that jointly optimizes controller parameters and Lyapunov-certificate parameters in an online loop. It uses a Black-Hole-based calibration to contract the search region, constructs a binary representation for quantum optimization, and applies quantum imaginary time evolution to find optimal parameters, validated on nonlinear consensus and motor control examples.
AI.motivation: Conventional nonlinear control designs typically tune controller gains offline and verify stability separately, lacking a unified online optimization that jointly redesigns controller and Lyapunov-certificate parameters at successive decision epochs.
AI.method: The method features a two-step computational structure: (1) a Black-Hole-based calibration procedure to contract the continuous admissible search region around the current operating condition, and (2) a finite binary representation constructed only over the calibrated region. The objective is encoded from sampled nonlinear closed-loop evaluations, approximated by a local quadratic pseudo-Boolean surrogate, and mapped to an Ising-type Hamiltonian. Quantum imaginary time evolution explores the Hamiltonian, and candidate bitstrings are decoded into continuous parameters, then re-evaluated on the original nonlinear cost and Lyapunov penalties.
AI.result: The framework is validated on three examples: first-order nonlinear consensus, second-order nonlinear consensus, and induction-motor drive control, demonstrating the feasibility of quantum-assisted co-design for nonlinear closed-loop systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dynamic quantum-assisted co-design framework successfully unifies performance improvement and Lyapunov-based stability synthesis within a single online optimization loop, accommodating different Lyapunov decay specifications by modifying the stability penalty, and is supported by open-source implementation code.

title: Analysis of a Competitive Bivirus SIS Epidemic Model with Game Theoretic Social Distancing
summary: We propose a competitive bi-virus model with dynamic social distancing behavior. Our model illustrates how public perception of different viruses changes the conditions for their eradication, their coexistence, or the dominance of one over the other. We show that our model is not monotone, in contrast to the classic bi-virus model. We detail how social distancing behavior produces different sets of equilibria than the classic bi-virus model and changes the criteria for their stability. In particular, we detail the set of disease free equilibria (DFE) present in our model and identify necessary and sufficient conditions for almost global exponential stability of the same. We prove similar global results for all but one non-DFE isolated (unilateral) equilibria and local stability results for the remainder. We also consider coexistence equilibria; we show such equilibria, when they exist, take the form of lines of equilibria and give local conditions for their stability. Finally, we illustrate our theoretical findings with numerical examples.

AI.tldr: A competitive bi-virus model incorporating dynamic social distancing behavior is proposed, showing how public perception alters virus eradication, coexistence, and dominance conditions, with analysis of equilibria and stability.
AI.motivation: To understand how social distancing behavior, driven by public perception of different viruses, changes the dynamics and equilibrium outcomes of competing viruses compared to classic bi-virus models.
AI.method: Develops a competitive bi-virus model with dynamic social distancing behavior; analyzes equilibria (disease-free, unilateral, coexistence) and their stability using mathematical proofs (global exponential stability, local stability) and numerical examples.
AI.result: The model is non-monotone (unlike classic bi-virus models); produces different equilibrium sets; identifies necessary and sufficient conditions for almost global exponential stability of DFE; proves global results for non-DFE unilateral equilibria and local results for others; shows coexistence equilibria form lines of equilibria.
AI.conclusion: Social distancing behavior fundamentally alters bi-virus competition outcomes, yielding novel equilibrium structures (e.g., lines of equilibria) and stability criteria distinct from classic models.

title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
summary:
To unleash the full potential of AI for Science, we must untether the agents from a purely digital environment. The agent's ability to control and explore in real-world labs is essential because the physical lab remains foundational to scientific discovery. While some tasks can be performed on a computer (e.g., data analysis, running simulated experiments), Eureka moments could occur at any time while operating lab instruments (e.g., when a scientist notices unexpected clues, intuition may prompt a real-time course change). Although autonomous labs are on the rise, which expose programmable APIs to control scientific instruments via software, bridging the gap between increasingly powerful AI agents and automated lab equipment requires innovation that draws insights from computer systems.
  We propose a new paradigm called ``Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs,'' where a core concept is to encode experiments as declarative configurations that can be compiled down to device-level APIs. AI agents come up with hypotheses and experiments, written as an ensemble of declarative configurations. The systems layer performs program analysis, safety checks, resource assignment, and job orchestration. Finally, programmatic experimentation occurs via actuating the device APIs. This is a general stack that is science-, lab-, and instrument-independent, representing a novel synthesis across the physical, systems, and intelligence layers to unleash the next breakthrough in AI for Science.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs," a paradigm where scientific experiments are encoded as declarative configurations that can be compiled to device-level APIs, enabling AI agents to autonomously control and explore real-world lab instruments through a systems layer that handles safety, resource management, and orchestration.
AI.motivation: Current AI for Science is limited to digital environments (data analysis, simulations), but real scientific discovery requires physical lab experimentation where serendipitous "Eureka" moments occur. There's a gap between powerful AI agents and emerging automated lab equipment that needs bridging.
AI.method: The method is "Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs," a general stack with: (1) AI agents generate hypotheses and experiments as declarative configurations; (2) a systems layer performs program analysis, safety checks, resource assignment, and job orchestration; (3) programmatic experimentation via actuating device APIs. Experiments compile down from declarative configs to device-level APIs.
AI.result: A proposed architecture that is science-, lab-, and instrument-independent, synthesizing physical, systems, and intelligence layers to enable autonomous AI-driven experimentation in real-world labs.
AI.conclusion: The EaC paradigm represents a novel cross-layer synthesis needed to unleash the next breakthrough in AI for Science by connecting AI agents to physical lab equipment through a robust systems stack.

title: Adaptive MPC for Constrained Trajectory Tracking of Uncertain LTI System with Input-Rate Limits
summary: This paper addresses the trajectory-tracking problem for discrete-time linear time-invariant systems with bounded parametric uncertainty, subject to hard constraints on system states, control inputs, and input rates. Unlike existing methods, which often consider only partial uncertainty, omit input-rate or state constraints, or focus on regulation problems, this work provides a systematic adaptive model predictive control (MPC) solution for constrained trajectory tracking under full parametric uncertainty. Determining the control input required to achieve zero tracking error under unknown parameters is challenging. Simultaneously, trajectory tracking under uncertainty with input-rate constraints induces temporal coupling in the control sequence, resulting in a time-varying admissible control set and rendering standard recursive feasibility arguments inapplicable. These challenges are overcome by systematically utilizing the estimated system parameters, coupled with a suitably designed adaptive learning process within a reformulated MPC framework. The recursive feasibility of the proposed MPC optimization routine is then rigorously established despite the time-varying admissible control set induced by input-rate constraints. Closed-loop stability is guaranteed via Lyapunov-based analysis, ensuring convergence of the tracking error and boundedness of system states. Simulation results validate the effectiveness of the pr

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic adaptive MPC solution for constrained trajectory tracking in discrete-time LTI systems with bounded parametric uncertainty, addressing hard constraints on states, control inputs, and input rates, with proven recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for trajectory tracking under uncertainty often consider only partial uncertainty, omit input-rate or state constraints, or focus on regulation problems. A systematic solution for constrained trajectory tracking under full parametric uncertainty is lacking.
AI.method: The proposed method reformulates the MPC framework by systematically utilizing estimated system parameters with an adaptive learning process. It addresses temporal coupling from input-rate constraints that cause time-varying admissible control sets, and establishes recursive feasibility and Lyapunov-based stability guarantees.
AI.result: Simulation results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, demonstrating convergence of tracking error and boundedness of system states.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive MPC framework successfully handles trajectory tracking under full parametric uncertainty with state, input, and input-rate constraints, with rigorous guarantees on recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability.

title: Towards Lag Consensus with Noisy Digital Twins Perception in Second-order Multi-agent Cyber-physical Systems
summary: In this paper, we study second-order lag consensus in multi-agent cyber-physical networks subject to random noise and input failures, within a framework modeling the interactions and perceptions between physical twins and digital twins. We propose a lag consensus protocol and establish sufficient conditions for the mean-square (exponential) stability of the resulting stochastic lag error dynamics. The consensus criteria are derived via Lyapunov analysis using the Itô formula, ensuring robustness to random perturbations and intermittent input failures. Numerical examples illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper studies second-order lag consensus in multi-agent cyber-physical networks with random noise and input failures, using a physical-digital twin framework, and establishes mean-square stability conditions via Lyapunov-Itô analysis.
AI.motivation: To achieve lag consensus in multi-agent cyber-physical networks despite random noise and input failures, within a physical-digital twin interaction framework.
AI.method: Proposes a lag consensus protocol and uses Lyapunov analysis with the Itô formula to derive sufficient conditions for mean-square (exponential) stability of stochastic lag error dynamics.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for mean-square (exponential) stability of the stochastic lag error dynamics are established, ensuring robustness to random perturbations and intermittent input failures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively achieves robust lag consensus under noise and failures, validated by numerical examples.

title: From open-loop representations to closed-loop feedback implementations in differential games: A numerical case study
summary: Solutions to pursuit-evasion and surveillance-evasion differential games are typically computed and expressed using open-loop representations, with the synthesis of feedback strategies significantly less common. We propose a numerical scheme for obtaining feedback strategies for the recently introduced prying-pedestrian surveillance-evasion differential game. The scheme involves computing feedback strategies as input-output maps approximated via neural networks trained using data obtained from open-loop representations of solutions. Simulations show the effectiveness of neural networks trained with an appropriate learning-loss function. Since optimal feedback strategies are discontinuous, as a second contribution, the potential loss/gain of individual players is subsequently studied for players using sample-and-hold feedback compared to continuous-time feedback.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a numerical scheme to compute feedback strategies for a surveillance-evasion differential game by training neural networks on open-loop solution data, and analyzes the loss/gain when using sample-and-hold feedback versus continuous-time feedback due to strategy discontinuities.
AI.motivation: Feedback strategies for pursuit-evasion and surveillance-evasion differential games are rarely synthesized, while open-loop representations dominate. The authors aim to bridge this gap for the prying-pedestrian surveillance-evasion game.
AI.method: The scheme computes feedback strategies as input-output maps approximated via neural networks trained on data from open-loop solution representations. A suitable learning-loss function is used.
AI.result: Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the neural network approach with an appropriate loss function. The study also quantifies the loss/gain when players use sample-and-hold feedback versus continuous-time feedback, motivated by the discontinuity of optimal feedback strategies.
AI.conclusion: Neural networks trained on open-loop data can effectively approximate discontinuous feedback strategies, and the sample-and-hold implementation introduces measurable performance trade-offs compared to continuous-time feedback.

title: Equilibrium points and stability of synchronous machine systems
summary: This paper investigates equilibrium points and stability in two synchronous machine configurations: (i) a single generator with an impedance load and (ii) two interconnected machines with co-located loads. We consider both abc and dq reference frames to show that the equilibrium condition reduces to a cubic polynomial in the single-machine case and to an 18th- degree polynomial in the two-machine case. For the single-machine system, Lyapunov stability analysis and linearization based stability analysis are carried out. For the two-machine system, local stability is assessed through linearization and eigenvalue analysis. Illustrative examples confirm the existence of multiple equilibria and illustrate the impact of parameter variation on stability. Our results provide insight into the stability of synchronous machine systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies equilibrium points and stability in single and two synchronous machine systems, deriving polynomial equilibrium conditions (cubic for one machine, 18th-degree for two machines) and analyzing stability via Lyapunov methods, linearization, and eigenvalue analysis across abc/dq reference frames.
AI.motivation: To understand equilibrium points and stability characteristics of synchronous machine systems in both single-generator and interconnected configurations, addressing the complexity of multiple equilibria and parameter sensitivity.
AI.method: Equilibrium conditions derived in abc and dq reference frames reduce to polynomial equations (cubic for single-machine, 18th-degree for two-machine). Stability analyzed via Lyapunov theory and linearization-based eigenvalue analysis.
AI.result: Multiple equilibria exist in both configurations; parameter variations significantly impact stability; the two-machine case yields a high-degree (18th) polynomial equilibrium condition.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide valuable insights into synchronous machine system stability, demonstrating the complexity of interconnected systems and the importance of reference frame selection in analysis.

title: Negative Imaginary and Passivity Properties of Synchronous Machine Systems
summary: The recent rapid proliferation of renewable energy is fundamentally changing the dynamic operations of power systems, necessitating new approaches to assess stability for these highly nonlinear systems. In this paper, we prove that synchronous machine systems, modeled in the nonlinear dq-frame, possess fundamental dissipativity properties. Specifically, we show passivity from current input to voltage output and a nonlinear negative imaginary property from torque input to rotor angle output. For the nonlinear system shifted around an equilibrium point, we derive explicit conditions for both passivity and the NI property to hold. Finally, we demonstrate that interconnection with passive droop controllers preserves these dissipativity properties with identical supply rates, thereby ensuring closed-loop stability.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that synchronous machine systems modeled in nonlinear dq-frame have fundamental dissipativity properties (passivity and negative imaginary), derives explicit conditions for these properties, and shows that interconnection with passive droop controllers preserves stability.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of renewable energy is changing power system dynamics, requiring new approaches to assess stability for highly nonlinear systems.
AI.method: The paper proves dissipativity properties (passivity from current input to voltage output, nonlinear negative imaginary from torque input to rotor angle output) in nonlinear dq-frame models of synchronous machines, and derives explicit conditions for shifted systems around equilibrium points.
AI.result: Synchronous machine systems exhibit passivity and nonlinear negative imaginary properties under explicit conditions, and these properties are preserved when interconnected with passive droop controllers.
AI.conclusion: Interconnection with passive droop controllers preserves dissipativity properties with identical supply rates, ensuring closed-loop stability for renewable-rich power systems.

title: Toward less conservative distributed stability analysis of power systems via matrix-valued differential passivity indices
summary: Passivity indices have been widely adopted to derive distributed stability certificates for power systems. Nevertheless, conventional passivity indices remain scalar-valued even for multi-input-multi-output (MIMO) systems, which can introduce excessive conservatism and compromise analysis accuracy. To overcome these limitations, this paper extends the differential passivity index to a matrix-valued formulation that captures both channel-wise passivity properties and inter-channel coupling effects in MIMO subsystems. On this basis, semi-distributed and fully distributed stability criteria are developed for power systems with heterogeneous nonlinear devices. It is shown that system stability is guaranteed when the aggregate passivity excess of devices compensates for the passivity shortage imposed by the network. Furthermore, analytical passivity matrix expressions for typical power system components are derived, facilitating compositional stability analysis. Case studies on a three-bus system and a modified IEEE 118-bus system validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: This paper extends differential passivity indices to a matrix-valued formulation for MIMO power system components, capturing inter-channel coupling effects, and develops semi-distributed and fully distributed stability criteria validated on test systems.
AI.motivation: Conventional scalar-valued passivity indices for MIMO power systems introduce excessive conservatism and compromise analysis accuracy because they fail to capture inter-channel coupling effects.
AI.method: Extends differential passivity index to a matrix-valued formulation; develops semi-distributed and fully distributed stability criteria; derives analytical passivity matrix expressions for typical power system components.
AI.result: System stability is guaranteed when aggregate passivity excess of devices compensates for the passivity shortage imposed by the network. Validated on a three-bus system and a modified IEEE 118-bus system.
AI.conclusion: The proposed matrix-valued passivity framework reduces conservatism compared to scalar indices and enables compositional stability analysis for power systems with heterogeneous nonlinear devices.

title: ADMM-based decomposed DNN+RLT Relaxations for Completely Positive Models in Electricity Market Clearing
summary: The day-ahead electricity market clearing with nonconvex order types can be formulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP), but its LP relaxation may provide weak bounds, and exact solutions can become computationally intractable in large-scale or extended market settings. We study a welfare-maximizing clearing model with elementary hourly orders, block orders with logical acceptance constraints, and flexible hourly orders. Starting from a compact MILP formulation, we derive an equivalent completely positive programming (CPP) reformulation via matrix lifting and propose relaxed CPP variants that further reduce the modeling burden while maintaining strong bounds. We then develop tractable doubly nonnegative (DNN) relaxations, including decomposed formulations that exploit the problem structure by using smaller positive semidefinite matrices. To further strengthen these bounds, we introduce reformulation-linearization technique (RLT) inequalities tailored to the decomposed structure. To tackle the challenge of large-scale DNNs, we design an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) with adaptive penalty updates and rigorous dual lower bounds, enabling certified early termination. Computational experiments on synthetic instances show that the proposed DNN+RLT relaxations substantially tighten LP bounds, while decomposition and first-order methods significantly reduce computational effort.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes doubly nonnegative (DNN) relaxations with RLT inequalities and an ADMM solver to strengthen LP bounds and efficiently solve the nonconvex day-ahead electricity market clearing MILP problem.
AI.motivation: The LP relaxation of the MILP formulation for day-ahead electricity market clearing with nonconvex orders provides weak bounds, and exact MILP solutions are computationally intractable in large-scale or extended market settings.
AI.method: The authors derive a completely positive programming (CPP) reformulation via matrix lifting from a compact MILP, develop tractable doubly nonnegative (DNN) relaxations with decomposed formulations using smaller PSD matrices, introduce RLT inequalities tailored to the decomposed structure, and design an ADMM with adaptive penalty updates and certified early termination.
AI.result: The proposed DNN+RLT relaxations substantially tighten LP bounds, while decomposition and first-order methods significantly reduce computational effort on synthetic instances.
AI.conclusion: The DNN+RLT approach combined with ADMM provides a practical and certifiably tight relaxation framework for large-scale nonconvex electricity market clearing problems.

title: Adaptive Contention-based Random Access for Uplink Reporting in 3GPP Ambient IoT Networks
summary: Ambient Internet of Things (A-IoT) targets energy harvesting (EH), battery-less devices as a simple connectivity solution for extensive ultra-low-power deployments. These devices typically face intermittent energy availability, making uplink reports increasingly susceptible to access collisions and energy outages. In this paper, we build upon the cellular standardization of A-IoT and examine the paging-triggered contention-based random access (CBRA) framework for uplink reporting. We analyze the effects of energy availability and collisions on these systems and introduce an EH-aware access control mechanism. In this mechanism, the reader broadcasts an access probability in the paging message, which helps regulate the number of devices attempting random access. Results show that, unlike the baselines, the proposed method scales well under dense deployments by keeping collisions nearly constant, improving access efficiency, and substantially reducing the number of paging rounds required for successful reporting. These results highlight the importance of lightweight reader-side access control for reliable and resource-efficient reporting in A-IoT environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an energy-harvesting-aware access control mechanism for Ambient IoT (A-IoT) that uses paging-triggered contention-based random access (CBRA). By broadcasting an access probability in paging messages, the method reduces collisions, improves access efficiency, and reduces paging rounds needed for successful uplink reporting in dense, battery-less deployments.
AI.motivation: A-IoT devices are battery-less and energy-harvesting dependent, leading to intermittent energy availability and high collision risks during uplink reporting. Existing solutions lack effective access control accounting for both energy constraints and collision dynamics in dense deployments.
AI.method: The authors build on cellular A-IoT standardization, analyze the paging-triggered CBRA framework with energy availability and collision effects, and introduce an EH-aware access control mechanism where the reader broadcasts an access probability in the paging message to regulate the number of devices attempting random access.
AI.result: Unlike baselines, the proposed method scales well in dense deployments, keeps collisions nearly constant, improves access efficiency, and substantially reduces the number of paging rounds needed for successful reporting.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight reader-side access control is crucial for reliable and resource-efficient uplink reporting in A-IoT environments, demonstrating that EH-aware probability-based regulation effectively mitigates collision and energy challenges.

title: Unlocking Embodied Probabilistic Computational Features in Motor Drives
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for publication in 2026 International Power Electronics Conference, IPEC-Nagasaki 2026 -ECCE Asia-
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven fault diagnosis in motor drives often requires significant computational efforts and time for re-training, in addition to the limited knowledge behind the model and suitability of training and learning mechanisms. This work bridges this gap by proposing a structured mechanism of transforming untapped labeled fault data into AI parameters to leverage probabilistic data-driven learning. This novel AI reservoir modeling framework for power electronics not only eliminates exogenous efforts behind learning data patterns and its optimization, but also provides intuitive guidelines for power electronics engineers behind sizing of AI models. This alignment between data and system physics makes the proposed model transparent and interpretable, bridging practical understanding with data-driven learning. Its computational efficiency is demonstrated using experimental data that structured, physics-aware reservoirs achieve higher diagnostic accuracy and clearer explanations than conventional black-box AI methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes a physics-aware reservoir modeling framework for AI-driven fault diagnosis in motor drives that transforms labeled fault data directly into AI parameters, eliminating retraining needs and providing transparent, interpretable models with higher accuracy than black-box methods.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-driven fault diagnosis in motor drives requires significant computational effort and time for re-training, suffers from limited model interpretability, and lacks clear guidelines for AI model sizing tailored to power electronics applications.
AI.method: A structured mechanism transforms untapped labeled fault data into AI parameters using probabilistic data-driven learning, creating a physics-aware reservoir modeling framework that aligns data with system physics for transparency and interpretability.
AI.result: Experimental data demonstrates that the proposed physics-aware reservoirs achieve higher diagnostic accuracy and clearer explanations compared to conventional black-box AI methods, while eliminating exogenous learning and optimization efforts.
AI.conclusion: The structured, physics-aware reservoir framework provides an efficient, interpretable, and transparent alternative to black-box AI for motor drive fault diagnosis, bridging practical engineering understanding with data-driven learning.

title: Quantized Probabilistic AI for Gear Fault Diagnosis in Motor Drives
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for publication in 2026 International Power Electronics Conference, IPEC-Nagasaki 2026 -ECCE Asia-
summary: Deploying large artificial intelligence (AI) models in power electronics often demands high computational resources. Driven by the quantization paradigm, this digest proposes a quantization-aware training (QAT) principle to substantially minimize the number of bits required and simultaneously maximize the accuracy of computations in pre-trained AI models. Considering a pre-trained probabilistic Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) for gear fault diagnosis in motor drives as an example, we quantize its weights and activation functions from floating-point FP32 to low-precision INT8 values, which enhances the computational efficiency by a significant margin of 30-45% (for different model versions) without any compromise in the accuracy and uncertainty estimates. This substantiates a sustainable mechanism of deploying most quantized light-weight AI models into low-cost edge processors for power electronic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantization-aware training (QAT) method to compress pre-trained Bayesian Neural Networks from FP32 to INT8 precision, achieving 30-45% computational efficiency gains without accuracy loss in gear fault diagnosis for motor drives.
AI.motivation: Deploying large AI models in power electronics requires high computational resources, creating a need for efficient model compression techniques that maintain accuracy.
AI.method: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is applied to a pre-trained probabilistic Bayesian Neural Network (BNN), quantizing weights and activation functions from FP32 to INT8 precision.
AI.result: 30-45% improvement in computational efficiency across different model versions without any degradation in accuracy or uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: QAT enables sustainable deployment of quantized lightweight AI models into low-cost edge processors for power electronic applications.

title: Kinematic Discriminants of Deceleration Behavior Modes in Car-Following: Evidence from NGSIM Trajectory Data
summary: Gap-closing rate and visual looming swap discriminative dominance depending on deceleration intensity - a finding that reconciles a long-standing conflict in the car-following literature and challenges spacing-centered assumptions in traditional driver behavior models. This study presents a two-stage analytical framework that distinguishes between information availability (kinematic variables measurable in the environment) and information utilization (variables that demonstrably separate driver behavioral patterns), applied to 1,060,119 valid car-following observations from the NGSIM trajectory dataset (2,932 vehicles). Six kinematic features are extracted, and deceleration events are detected under two threshold conditions (-0.5 m/s^2 and -0.3 m/s^2). K-means clustering identifies behavioral modes, and one-way ANOVA with eta-squared effect sizes ranks each feature's discriminative power. Three key findings emerge: (1) threshold selection fundamentally shapes behavioral inference - the stricter threshold yields three interpretable modes while the permissive threshold collapses these to two; (2) hard braking prioritizes gap-closing rate (eta^2 = 0.715) while moderate braking emphasizes visual looming (eta^2 = 0.574); and (3) spacing headway is negligible (eta^2 <= 0.014) across both thresholds. These findings provide empirically grounded candidates for perceptual cue prioritization and have direct implications for ADAS warning system design and autonomous vehicle control.

AI.tldr: This study reconciles a conflict in car-following literature by showing that gap-closing rate and visual looming swap dominance depending on deceleration intensity, using 1,060,119 NGSIM observations. Hard braking prioritizes gap-closing rate (η²=0.715) while moderate braking emphasizes visual looming (η²=0.574); spacing headway is negligible (η²≤0.014). The work challenges spacing-centered assumptions in traditional driver models.
AI.motivation: To resolve a long-standing conflict in car-following literature regarding which perceptual cues drivers prioritize, by empirically distinguishing between information availability and information utilization under different deceleration intensities.
AI.method: Two-stage analytical framework distinguishing information availability from utilization; six kinematic features extracted from 1,060,119 NGSIM car-following observations (2,932 vehicles); deceleration events detected under two thresholds (-0.5 m/s² and -0.3 m/s²); K-means clustering for behavioral modes; one-way ANOVA with eta-squared effect sizes for feature discriminative power ranking.
AI.result: (1) Threshold selection shapes behavioral inference (stricter: three modes; permissive: two modes); (2) hard braking prioritizes gap-closing rate (η²=0.715), moderate braking prioritizes visual looming (η²=0.574); (3) spacing headway is negligible across both thresholds (η²≤0.014).
AI.conclusion: Provides empirically grounded perceptual cue prioritization candidates; has direct implications for ADAS warning system design and autonomous vehicle control; challenges spacing-centered assumptions in traditional driver behavior models.

title: Minimizing the Expected Cost of Synchronization in Lossless Power Networks
summary: The reliable operation of large-scale electric power networks is increasingly challenging, particularly with the integration of stochastic renewable generation. In this work, we address the problem of minimizing network transients by optimally modifying the underlying network. We formulate the problem in terms of graph Laplacian matrices and show that, under certain assumptions, the problem is convex. We derive a linear matrix inequality whose feasibility guarantees the existence and uniqueness of phase cohesive steady-state angles; this condition can be directly incorporated as a convex constraint in the optimization framework and we provide several geometric interpretations of the optimization problem. The proposed method is validated on the IEEE 30-bus test system, where results demonstrate that our approach effectively identifies critical links on the network. Dynamic simulations show a significant reduction in network transients and overall improvements across several performance metrics. We explore the sparsity-optimality trade-off using a reweighted $\ell_1$ heuristic.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a convex optimization framework using graph Laplacian matrices to minimize transients in power networks by modifying network topology, validated on the IEEE 30-bus system with significant transient reduction.
AI.motivation: Reliable operation of large-scale power networks is increasingly challenging due to stochastic renewable generation, motivating the need to minimize network transients through optimal network modifications.
AI.method: Formulates the problem using graph Laplacian matrices; shows convexity under certain assumptions; derives a linear matrix inequality (LMI) for phase cohesive steady-state angles as a convex constraint; uses reweighted ℓ1 heuristic for sparsity-optimality trade-off.
AI.result: Validated on IEEE 30-bus system; effectively identifies critical network links; dynamic simulations show significant reduction in network transients and improvements across multiple performance metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convex optimization approach successfully reduces network transients by optimally modifying network topology, with the LMI condition ensuring phase cohesiveness and the ℓ1 heuristic enabling sparsity control.

title: Input-Output Specifications and Dynamic Droop Coefficients: Stability and Performance Conditions for Grid-Forming IBRs
summary: This paper proposes dynamic stability and performance conditions for grid-connected inverter-based resources (IBRs). To this end, we extend the notion of steady-state droop coefficients to dynamic droop coefficients to capture the small-signal dynamics of IBRs and synchronous generators (SGs). Notably, the dynamic droop coefficients can be obtained from input-output data collected at the unit's (e.g., IBR or SG) point of interconnection without requiring prior knowledge of IBR internals or controls structure. To obtain frequency stability conditions, this IBR model is combined with a lightweight dynamic transmission network model that accounts for uncertainty of line dynamics. The resulting stability conditions are highly scalable and, given a few key network parameters, can be verified at the unit level. To make the conditions practical and offer intuitive and illustrative interpretations, we map the frequency stability conditions to bounds on the Bode plot of the dynamic droop coefficient for two broad types of IBR responses. Moreover, our specifications on the dynamic droop coefficient (i) translate basic frequency control ancillary services into verifiable requirements, and (ii) provide insights into the much-debated question of how to certify an IBR as grid-forming (GFM). The results are illustrated using dynamic droop coefficients obtained using detailed simulations of GFM and GFL IBRs as well as SGs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes dynamic stability and frequency performance conditions for grid-connected inverter-based resources (IBRs) by extending steady-state droop coefficients to dynamic droop coefficients derived from input-output data at the point of interconnection, without needing IBR internal knowledge. These conditions are scalable, unit-level verifiable, and mapped to Bode plot bounds for different IBR responses, offering insights into frequency control ancillary services and grid-forming (GFM) certification.
AI.motivation: To develop practical, scalable stability conditions for IBRs that do not rely on internal IBR knowledge or control structure, and to provide intuitive frequency stability verification at the unit level while addressing the certification of grid-forming IBRs.
AI.method: The paper extends steady-state droop coefficients to dynamic droop coefficients using input-output data from the unit's point of interconnection, combined with a lightweight dynamic transmission network model accounting for line dynamics uncertainty. Stability conditions are mapped to Bode plot bounds for two broad IBR response types.
AI.result: The proposed dynamic droop coefficients enable scalable, unit-level verifiable frequency stability conditions that translate frequency control ancillary services into verifiable requirements and provide insights into GFM certification. Results are validated using simulations of GFM and GFL IBRs and SGs.
AI.conclusion: The conditions are practical, intuitive, and highly scalable, requiring only a few key network parameters for unit-level verification, and offer new perspectives on certifying IBRs as grid-forming.
